newsitem.title: UK: European bonds tipped as U.S. seen nearing peak.
newsitem.headline: European bonds tipped as U.S. seen nearing peak.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries have been driven higher by a wave of supportive factors recently but analysts said on Wednesday the rally was overstretched and a switch into Europe held more promise.
A shortage of supply, benign economic data and diminishing interest rate concerns have all sent the U.S. long bond yield to lows not seen since February.
The 10-year yield gap between U.S. T-notes and German Bunds has shrunk to its narrowest point since January. But further gains are seen as doubtful.
"I get the sense that those going long into the market now are getting the tail end of any rally," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London.
"I don't think we're going to get a sustained break below 6.5 percent on the 30-year."
The long bond was quoted at 101-05/32 by midsession for a yield of 6.54 percent, down from a recent peak of around 7.29 percent on April 11.

Analysts said data later on Wednesday, including June consumer prices, May industrial production and capacity utilisation should continue to confirm that the economy is cooling in the second half of the year and consumers are remarkably restrained.
"Consumer fundamentals are very strong and yet they don't seem to spending very much," Chester said.
The market may drive a little higher on the data but analysts said the Treasury market was getting too complacent about the economic slowdown.
There was still a chance that the Federal Reserve could move pre-emptively and raise interest rates at its next policy meeting on August 19, they said.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkin's testimony on July 22 will be studied carefully for any clues in that direction.

The front end of the yield curve -- the relationship between the maturity of debt and its corresponding yield -- steepened recently as yields declined, while the two-to-30-year sector has flattened as the long end outperformed.

"To get bullish from here you do really have to have the market start pricing in a really decent chance the Fed could cut within the next six months," said Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London.
"And for that you really have to start thinking the economy could have one or two negative quarters. The conditions for that just do not look to be in place."
With Treasuries at lofty heights, European bonds look more attractive, analysts said. Mark weakness could provide an opportunity to dip back into the German market.

Jim Fralick, director of European economics at Morgan Stanley in London, forecast the T-note/Bund yield gap to push out from current levels of three-quarters of a percentage point but one percentage point would be the maximum on a three-month view.
"It's going to need some strong data in August and September to do that," he said.
"The recent outperformance of the U.S. could be tested," he said. "The German sell-off may be looking a little bit overdone...and I would go for a move back into Europe at these levels."
